body:
Our public recruiting post asked agents to formalise claims we do not have.

## The error

Delfie's Moltbook intro post ([`e06b5458`](https://www.moltbook.com/post/e06b5458-f19e-4177-ba05-9b0c990af69f), item 3) asked for:

> A Lean 4 / Mathlib agent to formalize Hardy–Weinberg, the Price equation and Fisher's fundamental theorem **against our theorem claims**.

`fisher-ftns` exists. **Hardy–Weinberg and the Price equation do not.** `claim-sources/math-bio-claims/claims/key-claims.json` holds 21 claims:

- Fisher 4 — `fisher-ftns`, `fisher-kpp-speed`, `fisher-sex-ratio`, `fisher-infinitesimal`
- Turing 3 — `turing-ddi`, `turing-wavelength`, `turing-morphogen-hypothesis`
- Kimura 5 — `kimura-fixation-probability`, `kimura-substitution-rate`, `kimura-fixation-time`, `kimura-heterozygosity`, `kimura-neutral-theory`
- Hamilton 4 — `hamilton-rule`, `hamilton-haplodiploidy`, `hamilton-lmc`, `hamilton-senescence`
- Maynard Smith 5 — `maynardsmith-ess`, `maynardsmith-hawk-dove`, `maynardsmith-war-of-attrition`, `maynardsmith-twofold-cost`, `maynardsmith-hitchhiking`

A `delphi_graph` / `docs/claims.json` scan for `price|hardy|weinberg` in claim ids returns nothing.

This has downstream cost: `doctor_memory` built a concrete batch plan around Hardy–Weinberg as "the control case in the same batch" — unambiguous, against Fisher's ambiguity. That plan cannot run. Corrected publicly [here](https://www.moltbook.com/post/e06b5458-f19e-4177-ba05-9b0c990af69f).

## Also loose

The intro post says "the core theorems of population genetics (18)". The actual set is 21 claims spanning five thinkers, of which AGENTS.md says 16 have a recorded proof. Neither number is 18. Worth reconciling the headline counts in `README.md` / `AGENTS.md` / outreach copy.

## Proposed work

**1. Add Hardy–Weinberg and the Price equation as claims.** They are the two most conspicuous absences in a set that claims to cover the core of mathematical biology, and both are worth adding on their own merits. Same schema as the rest (`statement`, `notation`, `context` with assumptions and formal status, `kind`, `proposed_test`, `paper`, `see_also`).

Once present: Hardy–Weinberg is the unambiguous control for a Lean batch, and Price is the clean example of an identity that holds by construction.

**2. Add a formalization-multiplicity tag on theorem claims.** Requested by `doctor_memory`; committed to publicly. Values:

- `one` — a single formalization (Hardy–Weinberg, once added)
- `several` — non-equivalent formalizations, listed (`fisher-ftns`: partial-change vs total-change, per Okasha BJPS 59(3) 2008)
- `identity` — provable under the model's own boundary conditions, carrying no empirical content (the Price equation; and `thompson1917-ch07-10`, confirmed at 5.94–5.99 neighbours but forced by Euler's formula, with the random-Voronoi control also at 5.94)
- `contingent` — a claim a dataset can actually touch

Note this is a **queryability** gap, not an honesty gap: `fisher-ftns` is already labelled "(partial-change form)" and its `context` states it is "proved in this partial-change reading" and false for total change under dominance, epistasis, frequency dependence or a changing environment, citing Price 1972 and Ewens 1989. But that lives in prose — you cannot ask `delphi_search_claims` for theorem claims with several non-equivalent formalizations; you would read 21 context paragraphs.

The tag should land **before** any Lean work starts, so Mathlib gaps show up against a known classification rather than being discovered mid-proof.

**3. Expose the tag** in `delphi_search_claims` / `delphi_graph` output, and consider whether `theorem: true` should be suppressed or annotated for `identity` claims — untagged, they inflate the theorem count with results that carry no biological information.

The `thompson1917-ch07-04` downgrade (confidence 0.6 → 0.35, after the segmenter-bias null) is recorded in some artefacts but not others, and the **published** one still asserts the superseded verdict.

## Current state

**Has the revision** — `test-data/claim-tests/nanopubs/unsigned/thompson1917-ch07-04.trig`:
- `rdfs:label "Claim test of thompson1917-ch07-04: mixed, confidence 0.35"`, `delphi:hasConfidence "0.35"`
- `resource/activity/thompson1917-ch07-04--claim-test--revision-1 a prov:Activity`
- `prov:used` the pinned `segmenter-bias/summary.json` blob at commit `f8469f4`
- `prov:wasInformedBy` + `dct:contributor` → `moltbook-vina`, `moltbook-hivefound`, `moltbook-nanoswarm`, each a `prov:Agent` with `foaf:name` and the comment URL
- before/after preserved: "Before: 4 of 5 tissues conform (confidence 0.6). After: … (confidence 0.35)."

This is exactly right and matches what `test-data/claim-tests/README.md` specifies.

**Does not have the revision** — `claim-sources/cell-geometry/nanopubs/`:
- `unsigned/evidence-cell-geometry-thompson1917-ch07-04.trig` — still `"tester's confidence 0.6"`, pre-revision description, and a `rdfs:comment` caveat list with no mention of segmenter bias
- `signed/evidence-cell-geometry-thompson1917-ch07-04.trig` — same, **and it is signed**
- `nanopubs/manifest.jsonl` records it as published to the **test** registry on 2026-10-31T14:38:38Z as `https://w3id.org/np/RA7cXwDk_dDADMSeHrandLwNMsPn_pKmV3iQnK66WQBgA`, generator commit `e66117b`

## Why it matters

There is a published nanopub asserting a verdict we have publicly retracted — including on Moltbook, where the retraction is the thing that earned the contributor credits. Anyone resolving the trusty URI gets confidence 0.6 and a caveat list that omits the reason it was wrong.

Low stakes in that it is the **test** registry, not production. But the whole point of the nanopub layer is that the published record is the record.

## Fix

1. Re-run `claim-sources/cell-geometry/build/generate.mjs` so the evidence nanopubs pick up the revised `result.json` (verdict, confidence, caveats, and the revision as a `prov:Activity` with the three contributors, matching the claim-tests builder's output).
2. Re-sign and re-publish to the test registry; append to `manifest.jsonl`. Nanopubs are immutable, so this is a new record superseding the old one — check whether the generator emits a retraction / `npx:supersedes` link to `RA7cXwDk…` rather than silently publishing a second assertion.
3. Check `ch07-08` and `ch07-10` in the same directory for the same staleness (`ch07-08` was also affected: hexagon fraction inflated 0.27 → 0.30 on random Voronoi).
4. Decide whether `cell-geometry/build/generate.mjs` and `test-data/claim-tests/build-test-nanopubs.mjs` should share the revision-emitting code, since right now only one of them does it.

## Prevention

Nothing currently fails when `result.json` has a `revisions` entry whose verdict/confidence disagrees with an already-published nanopub for the same claim. A check in the release path (`npm run status`?) comparing `manifest.jsonl` entries against current `result.json` verdicts would catch this class.

body:
Follow-ups to the segmenter-bias null (`claim-sources/cell-geometry/results/segmenter-bias/`), which downgraded `thompson1917-ch07-04` from confidence 0.6 to 0.35. Three items, in dependency order. Prompted by `doctor_memory` and `nanoswarm` on Moltbook.

## 1. Measure the SNR of the real micrographs (blocks everything else)

`segmenter_bias.py` renders synthetic tilings at SNR 12 / 4 / 2, with a code comment asserting "Real micrographs here sit around 3-6". **That is an assumption someone typed, not a measurement.** We have never estimated the SNR of the actual images in `inputs/images/`.

Every downstream correction is anchored to this number, so it has to be measured per image first — wall/background contrast over local noise SD, using the same definition as the renderer (`contrast / sigma`).

## 2. Forward-model inversion instead of comparing to a floor

Proposed by `doctor_memory` ([comment](https://www.moltbook.com/post/9ff17185-86a8-42ec-9337-aa8951185f64)):

> the bias isn't a constant you subtract — it's a function of local wall geometry, so no single correction factor can rescue the original margin […] enumerate candidate ground-truth tilings, forward-render each at the real image's SNR, and ask which truth reproduces your observed junction statistics.

Our grass inference (49% T observed matches the segmented cell-files tiling at 48–59%, so true T is probably ~100%) is already this move done informally. Formalising it turns a bound into an error bar.

Work:
- Replace the four hand-built tilings with a **parameterised family** — file aspect ratio, cross-wall stagger, size CV as continuous knobs.
- Forward-render at the measured per-image SNR from item 1.
- Keep the region of parameter space whose *segmented* junction statistics reproduce the observed ones.

This is ABC with a hand-rolled summary statistic. Honest output is a **set over a coarse family, not a posterior over "the truth"** — the real tissue is not in the family. Still strictly better than a floor.

Related, cheaper: the bias is monotone across our three SNR points (brick-wall T 3% → 10% → 16% as SNR falls 12 → 4 → 2), so adding calibrated noise to a clean real image walks it along a measured curve. Three points is thin — want 5–6 before leaning on it.

## 3. Ridge-based angle measurement (no learned boundary model)

Trace walls from the intensity ridge and measure angles there, independent of Cellpose boundaries. Cautions from `nanoswarm`, already recorded on the test contract: blur alone curves ridges toward Y near a vertex, so skip the vertex and fit straight lines to each wall's ridge points in an annulus starting several wall-widths out; validate on synthetic tilings first with an annulus-radius sweep, reporting the radius at which brick-wall T fraction plateaus as the measurement floor.

### Merge-bias check — done, resolved

`doctor_memory` asked whether at 3 px walls the blur makes two walls of a narrow cell indistinguishable from one wide wall, which would make the ridge and segmenter failures correlated rather than independent. Computed:

- Modulation between two walls as a fraction of the 0.50 wall contrast: 0.01 at gap 1 px, 0.15 at 2, 0.31 at 3, 0.53 at 5, 0.64 at 8, saturating at 0.65 by ~10 px.
- Clears 1 noise SD for cells wider than ~1.6 px (SNR 12), ~2.6 px (SNR 4), ~4.6 px (SNR 2).
- 5th-percentile minor axis: cell-files truth 24 px, random-Voronoi truth 22 px; real images 24 (cornea), 25 (moss), 23 (grass), 37 (fly eye), 81 (Aloe).

So **under 5% of cells anywhere approach the merge limit** — the two pipelines' failures are close to independent. Caveat: real-image widths are measured on Cellpose masks, so they are conditioned on the segmenter not having already merged a narrow pair; only the synthetic numbers are non-circular.

Bonus discriminator: a merged pair is not only a shallower dip but a wider one — FWHM 7.9 px (gap 1) / 9.2 px (gap 2) versus 4.3 px for a true single wall. **The ridge pass should log per-wall width alongside the angle.**

## 4. Does the bias generalise beyond CPSAM?

Offered on Moltbook but not taken up: same images through plain Cellpose cyto3, StarDist and a watershed baseline, to see whether the 120°-imposition is model-specific or a property of learned boundary models generally. 12 synthetic + 8 real images; roughly an hour of GPU time.

body:
Our cell-geometry pipeline turns out to compute, verbatim, the two parameters clinical specular microscopy uses to grade corneal endothelial health. That is worth following up as a direction in its own right, and it comes with one hard blocker.

## The observation

`claim-sources/cell-geometry/analyze.py` computes `area_cv` and `frac_hexagons` to test Thompson's `thompson1917-ch07-08`. These are, respectively, **polymegethism** and **pleomorphism** (HEX) — reported by every Topcon / Konan / Nidek specular microscope alongside endothelial cell density, and used to decide whether a cornea will tolerate intraocular surgery.

Rough clinical bands: CV < 0.33 normal, > 0.40 a surgical-risk marker; HEX > 60% normal, < 50% abnormal; ECD < 1000 cells/mm² risk.

Our one human corneal endothelium image (`results/human-corneal-endothelium/`) reads **CV 0.299, HEX 66.7%** — normal on both. It was also the most Thompson-conforming tissue in the panel: junction angle SD 9.7° over 229 junctions, 0% T-junctions, 5.99 mean neighbours.

The framing: polymegethism and pleomorphism are a tissue ceasing to satisfy Plateau's rules. The tissue that best obeys Thompson's 1917 law is the one where departure from it is a diagnosis.

## The part that matters

Re-reading our own segmenter-bias null (`results/segmenter-bias/summary.json`) for these two statistics:

| Tiling | true CV → segmented | true HEX → segmented |
|---|---|---|
| random Voronoi (disordered, polymegethous analogue) | 0.616 → 0.563 | 0.269 → 0.296 |
| hexagonal lattice (ordered) | 0.005 → 0.008 | 1.0 → 1.0 |
| brick wall (ordered) | 0.000 → 0.006–0.009 | 1.0 → 1.0 |
| cell files | 0.212 → 0.198–0.200 | 0.586 → 0.582–0.601 |

Both errors on the disordered tiling point **toward healthier**, and the bias is ~zero on the ordered tilings and largest on the disordered one — i.e. largest exactly where the reading is clinically decisive.

Same-direction precedent from a different mechanism: Konan's automated method overestimates ECD in low-density glaucomatous eyes, and the authors warn it "may overlook risk of corneal decompensation" ([10.1007/s10792-021-02008-4](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10792-021-02008-4)).

## Scope discipline

- Hypothesis about a **class of model**, not a result about any deployed device.
- Specialist corneal segmenters are already good — Vigueras-Guillén et al. report MAE ≈1.3% on CV and ≈3.1% on HEX, several times better than built-in microscope software ([10.1038/s41598-022-18180-1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-18180-1)). The concern is narrowly about **generalist zero-shot** segmenters used because they are convenient.
- Our image is alizarin-red **ex vivo**, n = 1. Cell density is uncomputable (a Commons image has no micron scale); CV and HEX came free only because they are scale-free.

## Test contract (to pre-register)

- **Expected observation:** on specular images with expert manual cell-edge segmentation, CPSAM-derived CV is lower and HEX higher than the manual gold standard, with the gap widening as gold-standard CV rises.
- **Disconfirming observation:** the paired difference has no consistent sign, or does not depend on gold-standard CV, or is small relative to the clinical decision margins.
- **Admissible datasets:** specular microscopy images with expert manual cell-edge annotation, spanning normal and abnormal CV/HEX, known pixel size, licence permitting reuse, not images the segmenter was trained on.
- **Inference method:** paired per-image difference (CPSAM − manual) in CV and HEX; regression of that difference on gold-standard CV; headline metric = **how many eyes cross a clinical threshold (CV 0.33/0.40, HEX 60%/50%) in the reassuring direction**.

## Blocker

The obvious gold standard is the **Rotterdam** set — 50 eyes, expert manual segmentations, 1.038 µm/px, published as freely available at `rod-rep.com`. **That domain no longer resolves** (NXDOMAIN as of 2026-11-01). Needed: a mirror, or another specular set with manual cell-edge annotation.

Candidates not yet chased:
- Rotterdam UT-DSAEK (383 images) and the 1203-image guttae set — "available from the corresponding author on reasonable request".
- ESCRS Digital Health dataset listing: a 385-image Topcon SP-3000 set, healthy and diseased, downloadable zip.
- `jpviguerasguillen/corneal_endothelium_TVST` on GitHub — weights and example images only.

## Secondary, speculative

Clinical morphometry counts neighbours and areas; nobody scores the 120° condition itself. Guttae physically shoulder cell borders aside, so **junction angle SD and T-junction fraction should degrade before hexagonality does** — a potentially earlier marker. Healthy reference from our data: 9.7°. Needs someone who knows vision science to say whether this is already a known dead end.

## Note

No claim in the repo currently says anything about health, so this needs a new claim before it has somewhere to attach.

Posted as a pre-registration on Moltbook for criticism before any data is touched: https://www.moltbook.com/post/1154e21c-f9ec-4381-ae39-12f6546ab236

body:
## Why

The claim graph has no plant mechanics: `docs/claims.json` has zero hits for hygro-, pinecone, cellulose, bilayer or wheat awn, and almost nothing treating plants as mechanical objects. The plant hygromorph literature is short, quantitative and well tested, which is exactly the shape of claim this project wants. It is also the biological input to Lee Marom's compositional-design work (MIT, Buehler lab; we have already been in contact with her), which gives us an external user for the claims once they exist.

**Priority: high among claim-source work.** It scores on every axis the project cares about at once: the claims are mathematical and two statements can become Lean theorems; the biological data to test the central law are already published with the needed quantities (Quan et al. 2021), so no scouting is required; and it directly moves the headline number "math claims supported by data measured on organisms" (currently 2 of 162). Only the hackathon deadline ranks ahead of it; after that it should be the next claim source.

## Claim source: `claim-sources/plant-hygromorph-mechanics/`

Extract key claims, with LaTeX math and recorded formal status, in the style of `claim-sources/math-bio-claims/`, from:

- Reyssat & Mahadevan 2009, *Hygromorphs: from pine cones to biomimetic bilayers*, J. R. Soc. Interface 6:951. Bilayer curvature from differential swelling (Timoshenko 1925), scale opening angle, response time vs thickness.
- Elbaum, Zaltzman, Burgert & Fratzl 2007, *The role of wheat awns in the seed dispersal unit*, Science 316:884. Humidity cycles → directed bending from cellulose fibril arrangement.
- Forterre, Skotheim, Dumais & Mahadevan 2005, *How the Venus flytrap snaps*, Nature 433:421. Turgor-driven curvature change triggering a bistable elastic snap; closure time scaling.
- Armon, Efrati, Kupferman & Sharon 2011, *Geometry and mechanics in the opening of chiral seed pods*, Science 333:1726. Antisymmetric fibril angles → helical twist.
- Quan, Pirosa, Yang, Ritchie & Meyers 2021, *Hydration-induced reversible deformation of the pine cone*, Acta Biomater. 128:370. Measured geometry, layer thicknesses and curvature; the dataset for the test below.
- Marom, Tibbits, Zardini & Buehler 2026, *A category-theoretic framework from biological mechanics to engineered stimulus-response systems*, JMPS, [arXiv:2604.26367](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.26367), code at [lamm-mit/CategoryTheoryDesign](https://github.com/lamm-mit/CategoryTheoryDesign). Source of the compositional framing and of a few modelling assumptions worth recording as claims (slender-beam limit `w/L << 1` for pinecone scales; swelling coefficients independent of humidity).

Thompson's mechanics claims already in the graph are the natural neighbours (`thompson1917-ch01-05`, `ch02-02`, `ch16-03`, `ch16-04`, `ch16-05`, `ch16-10`): same beam theory, inverse direction.

## Lean

Two statements in Marom et al. are theorem-shaped in our sense (math only, nothing about organisms):

- `Dyn` is a category (their Appendix A.2): identities, associativity, closure of the simulation condition `dα_x(f(x,e)) = g(α(x), α_E(e))` under composition by the chain rule. Mathlib `CategoryTheory` applies.
- Timoshenko bilayer curvature `κ = C_geom Δε` with `C_geom` as in their eq. 16, and linearity of the twist reduction `Δε_12 = (ε_L − ε_T) sin 2φ`.

Record under a `lean/` folder following `claim-sources/thompson-growth-form/lean/INSTRUCTIONS.md`, so they count as `proof: lean` theorems.

## Data test on organisms

Pre-register one test in `test-data/claim-tests/`: Reyssat–Mahadevan's prediction of pinecone scale curvature from layer thicknesses and moduli against the Quan et al. 2021 measurements. That would be a `biological` verdict on a bilayer-curvature law; Marom's own validation data are on printed specimens (`physical`), not organisms.

## Done when

- `claims.json` and unsigned nanopubs exist for the source, loaded by `scripts/site/load-claims.mjs` and visible via `delphi_search_claims`.
- At least the `Dyn`-category statement compiles in Lean with no `sorry`.
- One pre-registered test with a `result.json`.
- The `Current numbers` table in README and `test-data/claim-tests/SUMMARY.md` regenerated.

## Context

Assessment of Marom's work and how it maps onto the repo: chat transcript of 2026-10-31 ("Lee Marom's work and delphisci"). Marom is also second author on the ScienceClaw + Infinite paper ([arXiv:2603.14312](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.14312)); its §8 asks for multi-agent systems that propose stimulus laws and filter them by the simulation condition, which is a propose → verify → log loop like `delphi_propose_claim` → Lean/data test → nanopub.

body:
## What

Expose the blind multi-provider rubric rating from #61 as tools on the live MCP server (`https://delphisci-mcp.fly.dev/mcp`), so any agent, ours or another team's, can point it at a repository and get back a Science Claw rubric rating from three providers, each assessor's highest-value improvement, and signed nanopubs on the test registry as the record. The pipeline exists in `scripts/release/self-assessment/build/` (pack → assessors → merge → generate → publish); this issue turns it into a service.

## Tools

- `delphi_rate_project({ repo, commit?, rubric?: "scienceclaw-rubric/0.1.0", builderProvider, captures?: [...] })` → `{ job, status }`. Clones `repo` at `commit` (default: default branch head) into a scratch dir, runs the capture list (default: the one in `build/pack.mjs` minus delphisci-specific MCP calls; a project may add shell commands from an allowlist such as `gh issue list`, `git log`, `cat <file>`), hashes the pack, fans out to the assessor roster excluding `builderProvider`, merges, generates nanopubs, signs and publishes to the **test** registry, stores the result. Async; returns a job id immediately.
- `delphi_get_rating({ job })` → the `SUMMARY.md` content as markdown plus `assessments.json`: per-criterion scores, points of 100, weighted totals, spread, `comparison_found`, each assessor's `highest_value_improvement`, nanopub trusty URIs.
- `delphi_list_ratings({ repo? })` → ratings this server has produced, so a repo can see its own trajectory across commits (our own re-run after the data freeze becomes the first row).
- `delphi_rubrics()` → available rubric versions with weights and anchors.

Write tools require the forum API key (`X-Claw-Api-Key`, same path as `delphi_forum_post`), so a caller is a registered agent and rate-limitable. Reads are open.

## Blindness, enforced rather than promised

Each assessor runs as a provider API call (OpenAI, Google, xAI), not a Cursor subagent, with the pack contents inlined into the prompt and no tools. It cannot read anything else because it has nothing else. The server records the exact prompt hash and the pack hash in the nanopub provenance. `assessor != builder` is enforced by excluding `builderProvider`; a job with fewer than two remaining providers is refused (BEST_PRACTICES §1).

## Secrets and cost

The live server holds no secrets today. This adds `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `GOOGLE_API_KEY`, `XAI_API_KEY` and the nanopub signing key (`NANOPUB_PRIVATE_KEY`, `NANOPUB_ORCID`, `NANOPUB_NAME`) as Fly secrets. Mitigations:

- Signing publishes to the **test registry only**. Promotion to production stays a human, local action in the owning repo. The server never calls the production registry.
- Hard caps: one job per repo per hour, 3 concurrent jobs, pack size cap (2 MB of text), per-job token budget, daily spend cap; counters in `mcp/metrics.mjs`.
- Captures run in a scratch dir with a command allowlist, no network except `git clone` and `gh`.
- If a secret is missing the tools register but return "rating disabled on this server" instead of failing at call time.

## Layout

- `mcp/rate.mjs`: tool handlers, job store (SQLite like the forum), provider adapters.
- Move the reusable parts of `scripts/release/self-assessment/build/` into `mcp/rating/` (pack, merge, generate, publish) and have the repo-local scripts import them, so there is one pipeline.
- `mcp/README.md`: tool docs, blindness statement, caps.
- Our own re-run after the freeze (#61) goes through the server, which is also its first end-to-end test.

## Deliverables

- [ ] Provider adapters for the three assessors returning the `INSTRUCTIONS.md` JSON shape, validated by `merge.mjs`
- [ ] `delphi_rate_project`, `delphi_get_rating`, `delphi_list_ratings`, `delphi_rubrics` registered in `mcp/server.mjs`, documented in `mcp/README.md`
- [ ] Job store + caps + metrics
- [ ] Fly secrets set, deploy, `/healthz` reports rating enabled
- [ ] Rate `fractastical/delphi` through the live server and compare with the local #61 run (same pack hash → should reproduce scores within spread)
- [ ] Post on the forum offering it to other teams; any team that runs it is a collaboration-bonus record (#41, with the trusty URI as proof)

Related: #61 (the local run), #62 (the comparison the assessors ask for), #41 (reuse by other teams).

body:
## Why

The blind rubric rating in #61 scored us 58/100 with the two 25% criteria dragging: **collective capability 3.3/10**, because no assessor could find a measured multi- vs single-agent comparison anywhere in the repo (#41 says two four-arm runs happened; no arm scores are committed). We also have five assessor models scoring thousands of claims and no table saying which assessor is well-calibrated against the data verdicts we now have. Both are measurement gaps, not capability gaps. This issue closes them with two artefacts.

## A. Assessor leaderboard (side-by-side)

A table and a page in `docs/` ranking every assessor model we have used (GPT-5.6 Sol, Gemini 4 Argon, Grok 4.7, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5 and any truth-score models in `test-data/truth/`) against ground truth we already own:

- **Ground truth:** the 133 claims with a data verdict (`docs/claims.json` `evidence`: supports / refutes / mixed / inconclusive), the 47 Lean-checked claims, and the 109 live MorphoEval audits. Decisive subset = supports vs refutes (the 99 used in `plugins/fittest/README.md`).
- **Per assessor, per rubric version:** coverage (claims scored), accuracy and Brier score of its truth/resolvability score against the decisive verdicts, calibration curve (reliability bins), agreement with each other assessor (Cohen's κ per dimension), mean absolute difference from the assessor mean, and cost/latency from the subagent transcripts in `chats/subagents/` where recorded.
- **Pair and ensemble rows:** every assessor pair and the full ensemble (mean score, and the disagreement-routed rule from `plugins/fittest/route.py`), so the table itself answers "does adding assessors help": a single-assessor row that beats the ensemble row is a finding, not a bug.
- **Side-by-side view:** pick a claim, see every assessor's score, verdict, rationale and the data verdict next to each other; `delphi_rank_claims` already has the data, this is a `docs/leaderboard.html` built by `scripts/site/`.

Scores under different rubric versions are not pooled (BEST_PRACTICES §1). Output: `test-data/leaderboard/leaderboard.json` + `SUMMARY.md`, regenerated by the site build, and an MCP view (`delphi_rank_claims` gains `view: "assessors"` or a new `delphi_leaderboard`).

## B. Blinded single-agent replay baseline

The comparison the judges ask for, run on the work we actually did rather than a toy task. Every chat in `chats/` records every user prompt with its timestamp, and which subagents the collective spawned. That is a replayable transcript of the collective's inputs.

**Protocol (pre-register before running, commit the protocol first):**

1. **Pick replay units.** Chats where the user gave few prompts and the collective did a lot, e.g. [Darwin claims as nanopubs](chats/2026-10-30_1900_darwin-s-origin-of-species-claims-as-nanopubs.md) (2 user messages, 22 subagents, result: 247 claims, 3 assessors, nanopubs on production) and [Thompson](chats/2026-10-30_2015_thompson-s-on-growth-and-form-claims-as-nanopubs.md) (6 messages, 32 subagents). Pick 3 units of different sizes.
2. **Single-agent arm.** Feed the same user prompts, in order, with the same repo state as at the chat's first timestamp (`git checkout <commit-before-chat>` in a worktree), the same `AGENTS.md`/`BEST_PRACTICES.md`, the same wall-clock budget as the original chat and a token/cost cap, to **one model with subagents disabled** (no `Task` tool, no cloud agents, no other MCP writers). Run it for each of at least two models, one of them the model the original orchestrator used. The replay agent is blind: it does not get the original chat's assistant replies, the resulting commits, or anything after the chat's start commit; the worktree branch is isolated and never merged.
3. **Isolated-workers arm (optional, if time):** same prompts, subagents allowed but no shared state (no forum, no MCP, no shared files between subagents) to separate "parallelism" from "coordination".
4. **Score both arms the same way**, by assessors that are not the builder of either arm (BEST_PRACTICES §1), blind to which arm produced the output: number of claims extracted with a verbatim source quote that actually appears in the source text (automatic), fraction of claims the blind assessor marks as faithful to the source, number of valid signable nanopubs (`nanopub-js` strict sign succeeds, no dummy data per BEST_PRACTICES §2), number of assessments from ≥2 providers, wall-clock, tokens, cost, and defects found by a post-hoc audit (hallucinated quotes, duplicated claims, broken IRIs). Report per unit and pooled.
5. **Commit everything:** protocol, the replay prompts file, the arm outputs (as branches or tarballs under `test-data/collective-comparison/<unit>/<arm>/`), the scoring JSON, and a `SUMMARY.md` with the comparison table. Nothing from an arm is ever published to a registry.

**What counts as a result:** a table with rows = arms, columns = the metrics above, per replay unit, with the protocol committed before any arm was run. A null or negative result (single agent matches the collective) is a valid result and gets reported the same way; the point is to measure, not to win.

**Tie-in with #41:** if the two 20-claim four-arm runs' arm scores still exist anywhere (local files, transcripts), commit them under the same directory as a fourth unit; if they do not, say so in #41 and treat this issue as the replacement.

## Deliverables

- [ ] `test-data/leaderboard/`: leaderboard.json, SUMMARY.md, build script in `scripts/site/`, `docs/leaderboard.html`, MCP view
- [ ] `test-data/collective-comparison/PROTOCOL.md` committed before any replay run, with the three replay units, prompts, budgets, models, metrics and the blind-scoring rule
- [ ] Replay prompts extracted from `chats/` into `test-data/collective-comparison/<unit>/prompts.json` (user messages + timestamps + start commit)
- [ ] Single-agent arm run for each unit with ≥2 models, outputs committed, never merged or published
- [ ] Blind scoring by non-builder assessors, `scores.json` per unit
- [ ] `SUMMARY.md` comparison table; one paragraph in README "Current numbers"; re-run the #61 rating afterwards to see whether collective capability moves
- [ ] One slide: the table

## Known limits to state up front

The collective had human prompts interleaved with its progress (the user reacted to what it produced); the single agent gets the same prompts without that feedback loop, which favours the collective. Mitigation: also report a "prompts-only" collective arm if one exists in the transcripts (chats with exactly one user message), and state the asymmetry in the summary. Compute cost of the replay is real; cap it in the protocol and record spend.

body:
## Goal

Have several independent agents (different providers, none the builder's) score where the project stands today against the [Science Claw judging rubric](https://scienceclawhack.ai/), and publish each rating as a nanopublication so the self-assessment is on the record with the same provenance as everything else we publish. Output: a ranked list of gaps to fix before slides are due Sunday 13:00, and a signed audit trail that judges (or other teams) can query.

## The rubric

Weights from scienceclawhack.ai (Judging section):

| Criterion | Weight | Judges ask |
|---|---:|---|
| Problem significance & complexity | 20% | How difficult, open-ended, consequential and scientifically meaningful is the problem? |
| Scientific/technical impact | 25% | What was actually achieved? Novel, meaningful, rigorous, potentially useful? |
| Decentralized agency | 20% | Are decisions and capabilities distributed across agents with distinct information, resources or capabilities? Can they coordinate and adapt without a central planner prescribing the whole trajectory? |
| Collective capability | 25% | Does organizing agents collectively add measurable capability? Shown by a comparison (multi- vs single-agent, collaborative vs isolated, decentralized vs centralized)? |
| Execution & validation | 10% | Functioning system, not a concept? Performance demonstrated with evidence, benchmarks or real-world validation? |
| Collaboration bonus | +10 (outside the 100) | Tool/agent reused by another team; data or experiments enabling another team's result; shared infrastructure. |

## What the assessors get

Blind, per BEST_PRACTICES §1: the rubric, and a fixed evidence pack. No builder triage, no other assessor's output. The evidence pack is the repo at a pinned commit plus:

- `README.md` "Current numbers" (as of 2026-10-31 20:44 UTC: 1702 claims, 880 live on production, 63 theorems of which 47 Lean-checked, 133 claims tested against data: 78 supports / 25 mixed / 21 refutes / 9 inconclusive, 13 pre-registered).
- `delphi_overview`, `delphi_claim_tests` (summary and `view: "candidates"`), `delphi_morpholib` (`view: "live"`) output, captured to files so every assessor sees the same thing.
- `scripts/exec/runs/latest.json` (reproduced / drifted / failed counts for executable claims).
- Agent-architecture evidence for the decentralization criteria: `AGENTS.md`, `BEST_PRACTICES.md` (assessor != builder, two providers, blind assessment), `forum/README.md` and a dump of the Science Claw forum, `plugins/agent/`, `COLLABORATIONS.md`, `chats/README.md` (which agents did what).
- Collaboration-bonus evidence: `COLLABORATIONS.md`, `plugins/fittest/README.md`, #57, MCP usage by other teams (`npx -y github:fractastical/delphi`), issue #56 (external MCP test report).

## Rubric file

`assessment/rubric.json`-style, new type `scienceclaw-rubric/0.1.0` (new version if any wording changes, BEST_PRACTICES §1). Per criterion: score 0–10, one-paragraph justification citing concrete files/IRIs/issue numbers, and `gaps`: the concrete changes that would raise the score. Plus a weighted total and the bonus scored separately. The assessor must also state explicitly for Collective capability whether it found a multi- vs single-agent comparison anywhere in the repo, because today I believe we don't have one and that is the 25% criterion.

## Assessors

At least three providers from the existing assessor roster (`claim-sources/*/assessment/assessors.json`: GPT-5.6 Sol, Gemini 4 Argon, Grok 4.7), run as subagents with the pack and nothing else. Claude is the builder for most of this repo and is excluded as assessor. Record model ids in the nanopub provenance as the per-claim assessments do.

## Nanopubs

One assessment nanopub per assessor, target = the project itself (the repo IRI at the pinned commit, not a claim). Assertion: the per-criterion scores and weighted total; provenance: assessor agent, model id, rubric IRI, evidence-pack hash; pubinfo: standard. Follow the existing `assessments-signed/` layout under a new `claim-sources/../project-assessment/` or `scripts/release/self-assessment/` directory (decide in the PR). Publish to the **test registry** first and commit signed files + manifest in the same step. Promote to production only with Joel's explicit OK (publishing signs with the ORCID key and is irreversible).

## Deliverables

- [ ] `rubric.json` for `scienceclaw-rubric/0.1.0` and `INSTRUCTIONS.md` for assessors
- [ ] Frozen evidence pack (files + SHA-256 manifest) at a pinned commit
- [ ] Three blind assessor runs, raw JSON kept under `raw/<assessor>/`
- [ ] Merged table: per-criterion scores by assessor, mean, spread, weighted total, bonus
- [ ] Signed nanopubs on the test registry, manifest committed
- [ ] A short "gaps" section in the issue: the three cheapest changes that raise the weighted total most, ranked, so they can be turned into issues or into Sunday work
- [ ] Re-run once after the data freeze (#53, Sun Nov 1 12:00) so the slides quote the final numbers

## Known weak spots to expect

Writing them down so the assessors' finding them is not a surprise: no quantitative multi- vs single-agent comparison yet (Collective capability, 25%); decentralization is mostly "different providers assess blind" and the forum, with a human in the loop for publishing; validation is strong on claims (133 data tests, 47 Lean proofs) but the system-level claim "the collective did better than one agent" is untested.

body:
[Fittest MCP](https://fittest-mcp.westus2.cloudapp.azure.com/) ([source](https://github.com/Pavel-Tk/fittest)) asks a swarm of ML interatomic potentials (MACE-MPA-0, AIMNet2, Orb-v3) to predict forces on a molecule and returns, per structure: which model to serve, a calibrated trust score with a 90% interval and the number of DFT labels behind it, and a `send_to_dft` flag with reasons. A structure is trusted only if every model supports its elements, the force disagreement σF is below a fixed threshold, and a Beta-posterior P(correct), learned from DFT labels on Transition1x reactions, is at least 0.5. It is calibrated for gas-phase C/H/N/O chemistry and says so when you are outside that domain.

Endpoint: `https://fittest-mcp.westus2.cloudapp.azure.com/mcp` (HTTP, no auth). Tools: `check_structures`, `explain`, `swarm_status`, `usage_stats`. Limits: 20 structures per call, 2–100 atoms, molecules only. Calls are logged anonymously (tool, salted client hash, counts, latency); structures and coordinates are not stored.

## Fit with delphisci

**Direct use is narrow.** None of our ~880 claims is decided by gas-phase C/H/N/O forces. The "molecular forces" claims in `thompson-growth-form` are continuum surface-tension arguments, the `levin-papers` bioelectric claims are about ion channels and tissues, and organism claims are out of scope. Plausible small pilots only:
- Thompson's claim that molecular homochirality could start from a non-vital asymmetric force (circularly polarised light). Fittest can't test the claim itself, but it could sanity-check MLIP energies for small chiral C/H/N/O molecules used in a supporting calculation.
- Small-molecule modulators in Levin's bioelectric work, where any `claim-tests/` computation needs conformer energies. Most of these contain Cl/S, which puts them outside Fittest's calibration; the out-of-domain warning is the useful part here.

**The pattern transfers well.** Our assessments have the same problem Fittest addresses: cheap assessors (LLM truth scores, dataset-resolvability) can fail silently, and the expensive check (an executable test in `exec/` / `claim-tests/`, a Lean proof, or human review) is budget-limited. Fittest's design maps directly:

| Fittest | delphisci |
|---|---|
| MLIP swarm | assessor models (GPT, Grok, Claude, …) |
| force disagreement σF | spread of assessor truth scores per claim |
| DFT label | `exec` result (reproduced / failed) or Lean proof |
| Beta-posterior P(correct) + label count | per-assessor calibration against claims that have an executable outcome |
| `send_to_dft` | `send_to_exec`: queue claim for a test or human review |

## Tasks

- [ ] Add `fittest` to `.cursor/mcp.json` alongside `indra-cogex`, with a note in `AGENTS.md` under "Other biology knowledge graphs" (scope: C/H/N/O gas-phase molecules only).
- [ ] Run `check_structures` on 3–5 small C/H/N/O molecules from the homochirality pilot. Record verdicts, served model and trust intervals, and decide whether it is worth a `claim-tests/` entry.
- [ ] Prototype the routing for assessments. For claims with both assessor scores and an `exec/runs/latest.json` outcome, compute assessor disagreement and a Beta-posterior P(correct) per assessor, pick a threshold, and list which claims would be flagged for exec/human review. Report how many silent failures (assessors agree and are wrong) it catches.
- [ ] Contact the Fittest author (Pavel-Tk) about two-way options: (a) reusing their calibrator design or code for assessor routing; (b) publishing Fittest verdicts and calibration as nanopub claims and assessments with provenance (model, DFT reference, label count), as a computational-chemistry pilot project.

## Acceptance

A short note covering what Fittest returned on the pilot molecules, plus a table for the routing prototype: claim × assessor spread × P(correct) × flagged × actual exec outcome. Nothing published to production from this issue.

Test report for the MCP server, as committed in #53 (Amit's row: MCP testing). **93 of 100 cases pass.** The full report, with every case, is on PR #36: [`validation/MCP-TEST-REPORT.md`](https://github.com/xX-its-amit-Xx/delphi/blob/delphi-hack-2026-10-31/validation/MCP-TEST-REPORT.md).

**Method.** All eight tools, taken from the server's own `tools/list`. 100 cases, run against the hosted server (`https://delphisci-mcp.fly.dev/mcp`) and against a local copy of `origin/main`. Every answer was checked against an independent index built by parsing the TriG files directly, with no SPARQL. Calls were paced under 55 per minute. Hosted latency: median 32 ms, max 257 ms. **The hosted server and local `origin/main` agreed on all 100 cases.**

| Tool | Passed |
|---|---|
| `delphi_overview` | 6 / 6 |
| `delphi_search_claims` | 15 / 15 |
| `delphi_rank_claims` | 14 / 14 |
| `delphi_get_organism` | 9 / 9 |
| `delphi_get_claim` | 10 / 12 |
| `delphi_graph` | 14 / 15 |
| `delphi_organisms` | 14 / 15 |
| `delphi_sparql` | 11 / 14 |

## Failures, most serious first

**F1. Local mode is broken on Windows — every `source: "local"` query fails.** One-line fix, verified.
- Repro (Windows, repo root): `node mcp/cli.mjs overview` → `Parser error at line 1 between columns 57 and 59: Unexpected escape character '\n'`
- Cause: `mcp/lib.mjs` line 73 builds each file's base IRI from `relative(REPO, f)`. On Windows that path contains backslashes, which are not valid inside a Turtle IRI.
- Fix: append `.replaceAll("\\", "/")` to that path. **With exactly this change, the local server matched the hosted server on all 100 cases.** This also breaks the `.cursor/mcp.json` stdio setup on Windows. The hosted server runs on Linux and is unaffected.

**F2. `delphi_get_claim` splices the id unescaped into an IRI.** `{"id":"fisher kpp speed"}` returns a raw parser error (`expected IRI parsing failed`) rather than `found: false`, which is what an unknown id returns. No working injection was built, and impact is bounded because the store is read-only and `delphi_sparql` already allows any read-only query. But the id is not validated, and callers see parser internals.

**F3. `delphi_sparql`: `ASK` crashes and `CONSTRUCT` gives an unclear error.**

**F4. `delphi_sparql`: a query whose text contains `PREFIX`, even inside a string literal, gets no default prefixes.**

**F5. `delphi_graph` and `delphi_organisms` silently ignore `source: "network"`** — they return local results without saying so.

**F6. A request body over 1 MB returns 502 with an empty body**, not the intended 413. Protocol-level, not a tool case.

Nothing in the server was changed by this test. Each failure has its smallest reproduction in the report. Happy to open a PR with the F1 fix if whoever owns `mcp/` would like one.

## Goal

Make the open problems in the graph queryable, so another agent or person can ask "what is unresolved here, and what would it take to resolve it?" and get claim ids back. Today that question can only be answered by reading JSON.

## What an open problem is (proposed, please edit)

A claim is open if its status is not settled:

- **Untested** (814 of 880 claims): no evidence nanopub yet. Ranked by dataset-resolvability, the claims with real data available are the ones ready to test.
- **Partial** (1): only part of the mathematical statement has been proved.
- **Contested:** assessors disagree on the truth score, or the claim has evidence on both sides.
- **Blocked:** testable in principle, but the data does not exist yet. The dropped and unresolvable datasets show where.

Refuted (2) and proved (63) claims are not open. Proof does not mean organisms satisfy the claim, though, so a proved claim whose empirical test is missing may still count as open (AGENTS.md, "Theorem is a proof status").

@kganjam this one is yours (see the roles in #53).

## Goal

A simulator that generates the actual forms the laws describe. Feed it a claim and its parameters, and it renders the shape, pattern or tiling the law predicts: a horn, a shell, a phyllotaxis head, a cell partition, a fish outline under a coordinate transformation, a cellular-automaton pattern. Each generated form can then be compared with real specimens of the organisms the claim names.

This turns "the law says X" into a picture and a measurable object (outline, mesh, lattice). That is the test, and it is also the demo.

## Starting set: laws that specify a form

Proved in Lean (the math is checked; the simulator shows whether the generated form looks like the organism):

| Claim | Law | Form to generate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `thompson1917-ch13-03`, `ch13-01`, `ch13-06`, `ch13-13` | Unequal growth at a constant ratio gives a logarithmic spiral | Horns, tusks, curved shells in 3D |
| `thompson1917-ch14-07`, `ch14-08` | Single genetic spiral gives Fibonacci parastichies | Sunflower heads, fir cones |
| `thompson1917-ch08-01` … `ch08-09` | Partitions of least area | Cell division sequences in flattened tissues |
| `thompson1917-ch07-04`, `ch07-09`, `ch07-11` | Walls meet three at a time; close packing gives hexagons and the bee cell | 2D froths, honeycomb |
| `thompson1917-ch17-08` | The two halves of a begonia leaf are similar figures | Leaf outlines |

Untested (here the simulator is the first test):

Splits the "choose an open model" task out of #4 into something with an owner and a measurable goal. Motivated by the token budget in #42.

## Why

Morpholib's instrumented 12-step run (`morphoeval/runs/2026-10-19-turing-morpho-loop.csv`) shows one two-pass loop is ~0.56M recorded LLM tokens, realistically 2–5M with builder context; 84% is the dual audit (step 7, 138k) and remediation (step 12, 335k). Deterministic steps are under 40 s CPU, no GPU. Looping the 880 claims on frontier models is $9k–35k. Moving the **builder** (steps 2–6 and 12) to an open-weight model on Nebius AI Studio and keeping two **frontier assessors** (step 7) cuts the frontier share to ~15% and keeps `assessor != builder` and the two-provider rule satisfied by construction.

## Tasks

- [x] Confirm Nebius credits and the OpenAI-compatible endpoint (#4).
- [ ] Pick two candidate open models (one large, one mid) and run them as builder on 3 claims that already have frontier-built tests in `claim-tests/` (one each from `darwin-origin`, `thompson-growth-form`, `wolfram-nks`).
- [ ] Audit all six outputs with the same two frontier assessors, blind. Compare scores and defect counts against the frontier-built originals.
- [ ] Record tokens, wall clock and cost per loop in a CSV with the morpholib column layout so the numbers are comparable.
- [ ] Decide: if the open-weights builder lands within ~10 points of frontier after one remediation pass, make it the default builder in `BEST_PRACTICES.md` and note the assessors stay frontier.
- [ ] Use it for the flying-fish packages that are startable now (#50, #44, #48) as the first real workload.

## Acceptance

A table: model × claim × audit score × tokens × cost, and a one-paragraph recommendation. Nothing published to production from this issue.

This is the one page we point other agents and people at when they ask "what do you need?". Every ask has a concrete deliverable, the claim ids it bears on, and the skills wanted. Take one by commenting here, or by offering on the matching `request` post on the Science Claw forum. Results get published as nanopubs linked to the claim, under your name. Negative results count.

Query everything first, no key needed: MCP `https://delphisci-mcp.fly.dev/mcp` (`delphi_search_claims`, `delphi_get_claim`, `delphi_rank_claims`, `delphi_get_organism`), or `npx -y github:fractastical/delphi`.

## The big one: build the flying fish Darwin predicted

Darwin, *Origin* ch. VI:

> it is conceivable that flying-fish, which now glide far through the air, slightly rising and turning by the aid of their fluttering fins, might have been modified into perfectly winged animals.

We want to work backwards from that sentence to a physical object: a 3D-printed (later bioprinted) wing that can be fitted to a flying fish (Exocoetidae, `gbif:2968`, NCBI `76072`) and extends its glide, then flaps. Nobody expects this to be finished at a hackathon. The point is that each step below is a real, scoped piece of science an agent can do today, and each one tests a claim already in the graph. Darwin and Thompson wrote the spec; we are asking for the engineering.

Claims this project tests directly:

| Claim | What it says | How the fish tests it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `darwin1859-ch06-05` | Bats derived from gliders; wing membranes are traces of gliding apparatus | Glider to flapper is the transition we are trying to engineer |
| `darwin1859-ch09-12` | Adapting to flight is slow, then radiates fast | Is there a small set of design changes after which many wing forms work? |
| `thompson1917-ch02-06` | Minimum flight speed scales as √(linear size); work for flight as size^3.5 | Sets the speed a fish of given mass must reach at launch |
| `thompson1917-ch02-07` | Beyond a size, muscle-powered flight with ordinary anatomy is impossible | Is a 300 g fish inside the envelope at all, and with what fin muscle? |
| `thompson1917-ch02-10` | Swimming, flight and walking give velocity ∝ √(size) | Exit velocity from water vs required airspeed, same scaling law |
| `thompson1917-ch16-01` | Fitness of form for swimming or flight can be analysed mechanically | The whole project is a test of this |
| `thompson1917-ch16-03` | Hollow cylinders where stiffness is needed, e.g. wing bones | Spar design for the printed wing |

### Work packages (each is a separate, claimable ask)

- [ ] #50 **WP1 Literature and data: what does a flying fish actually do?** Collect published glide data (Exocoetidae: take-off speed, glide distance, pectoral-fin area and aspect ratio, body mass, taxiing with the caudal fin) into one CSV with DOIs. Add it as a dataset record under `test-data/organisms/` for `exocoetidae` (currently only taxonomy and GBIF occurrences). *Skills:* literature search, biomechanics. *Tests:* `thompson1917-ch02-06`, `ch02-10`.
- [ ] #43 **WP2 Scaling check: is the fish inside Thompson's envelope?** Using WP1 numbers, compute the required airspeed for sustained glide and for powered flight vs. the fish's exit velocity and estimated pectoral muscle power, for body sizes across the family. Report where the glide-to-flight gap is, as a plot and a `result` nanopub. *Skills:* physics, Python/Julia. *Tests:* `thompson1917-ch02-06`, `ch02-07`, `ch02-10`.
- [ ] #44 **WP3 Wing morphology from real specimens.** Digitise pectoral fins (museum photos, iDigBio/GBIF media, CT scans if any exist) into planform outlines and camber; fit Thompson-style coordinate transformations between species (`thompson1917` ch. 17 claims). Deliverable: SVG/STL outlines plus the transformation grids. *Skills:* morphometrics, image processing.
- [ ] #45 **WP4 Aerodynamics: design the add-on wing.** Given the fish's mass and launch speed, design a wing (planform, camber, aspect ratio, attachment at the pectoral girdle) that raises lift-to-drag enough to extend glide measurably. XFLR5/OpenFOAM or a vortex-lattice code is fine. Deliverable: geometry, polars, and the predicted glide-distance gain. *Skills:* aerodynamics, CFD. *Tests:* `thompson1917-ch16-01`.
- [ ] #46 **WP5 Printable structure.** Turn WP4 into a printable part: hollow-spar design per `thompson1917-ch16-03`, mass budget, a flexible membrane material that survives salt water, and a non-injurious attachment. Deliverable: STL/3MF plus a Formlabs PreForm print profile (we have a Formlabs sponsor integration, #3). *Skills:* mechanical design, additive manufacturing.
- [ ] #47 **WP6 Test rig and protocol.** A rig that launches a dead specimen or a mass-matched dummy at the measured exit velocity, with and without the wing, and measures glide distance. Also the ethics and husbandry plan for any live work (this is where we stop until a lab with proper approvals joins). *Skills:* experimental design, animal welfare.
- [ ] #48 **WP7 Bioprinting path.** Scoping only: which bioprinted scaffold (fin-ray-like collagen/chitosan, or a hydrogel membrane) could replace the plastic membrane, who has the printer, and what the cell source would be. Deliverable: a two-page feasibility note with citations, and the names of two groups to ask. *Skills:* tissue engineering, bioprinting.
- [ ] #49 **WP8 Glide to flap.** The Darwin step: what actuation (fin muscle recruitment, or an external oscillator) would be needed to go from glide to powered flight, and does any scaling law forbid it at this body size. *Tests:* `darwin1859-ch06-05`, `thompson1917-ch02-07`.

### Tracker: what is needed to get to the flying fish

Dependency order (each arrow is "needs"):

```
#50 WP1 data ──┬──> #43 WP2 scaling ──┐
               │                      ├──> #49 WP8 glide-to-flap
               └──> #45 WP4 aero  ────┘
#44 WP3 fins ──────^   │
                       └──> #46 WP5 print ──> #47 WP6 rig + ethics gate ──> (live trial only with a partner lab)
#48 WP7 bioprint: parallel scoping
```

| WP | Issue | Status | Needs | Owner | Est. tokens | Compute |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 Glide data | #50 | in progress | nothing | @xX-its-amit-Xx | 0.5M | none |
| 2 Scaling test | #43 | pre-registering; comparison waits on WP1 | WP1 | @xX-its-amit-Xx | 1–2M | CPU seconds |
| 3 Fin morphology | #44 | open, startable now | nothing (better with WP1) | – | 1M | CPU |
| 4 Aero design | #45 | blocked | WP1, WP3 | – | 1–2M | XFLR5 minutes; 50–200 CPU-h if CFD |
| 5 Printable wing | #46 | blocked | WP4 | – | 0.5–1M | printer |
| 6 Rig + ethics gate | #47 | blocked | WP5 | – | 0.5M | rig materials, partner lab |
| 7 Bioprint scoping | #48 | open, startable now | nothing | – | 0.5M | none |
| 8 Glide to flap | #49 | formal half in progress; rest blocked | WP2, WP4 | @xX-its-amit-Xx (formal half only) | 1–2M | CPU |

Totals: ~6–10M tokens (≈ $60–400 depending on model tier), one CFD sweep, one print, zero live animals until WP6 is satisfied. Three packages (#50, #44, #48) need nobody's permission to start today. Update the status and owner columns here as people take packages; the per-issue thread holds the detail.

### Compute and credits

Measured on morpholib's instrumented 12-step run (`morphoeval/runs/2026-10-19-turing-morpho-loop.csv`): one two-pass loop is ~0.56M recorded LLM tokens (realistically 2–5M with the builder's context), under 40 s of CPU for all deterministic steps, no GPU. 84% of the tokens are the dual audit (step 7) and remediation (step 12). So the constraint on this project, and on looping the other 880 claims, is token credits, not GPU.

What that means for anyone taking a package:

- **Bring your own builder.** Run the build steps (2–6, 12) on whatever model you have; we run the two independent assessors (~140k tokens per loop) and publish the result as a nanopub under your name. `assessor != builder` is required anyway, so this costs nothing in rigour.
- **Builder on open weights.** We are moving our own builder to an open-weight model on Nebius (#4, tracked in #51) and keeping frontier models for assessors.
- **Credits we have or are chasing:** OpenResearch/alphaXiv GPU credits (#10, #16), Nebius (#4), Google Cloud (#7), OpenAI (#8). The one real compute item here is the WP4 CFD sweep.

## Standing asks (not fish-specific)

- [ ] **Biologist or morphologist** to say, per tissue, whether our Cellpose-SAM segmentations are a fair test of Thompson's surface-tension argument (grass epidermis and the curved SEM eye are the suspect ones). *Tests:* `thompson1917` ch. 7 cell-packing claims.
- [ ] **Phylogenetics agent** to run a comparative test (PGLS or similar) of trait claims across the 782 taxa resolved to GBIF/NCBI ids.
- [ ] **Lean 4 / Mathlib agent** to formalise Hardy–Weinberg, the Price equation and Fisher's fundamental theorem against our theorem claims (`math-bio-theorems/`).
- [ ] **Dataset-reliability scorers**: 1,372 vendored dataset records, five-dimension rubric, batches are independent.
- [ ] **Bioelectric time series**: any open V_mem recordings (planarian, Xenopus) to test the bioelectric claims.
- [ ] **Knowledge-graph partners** (INDRA, Monarch, nanopub community) via the MCP server, see #35 and #34.

## How to take one

1. Comment here with the WP number, what you will deliver and by when, or `node forum/client.mjs offer <postId>` on the matching request post on the Science Claw forum.
2. Put data under `organisms/<project>/.../datasets/` or results under the relevant project with provenance (source, date, method, model if any).
3. We publish the result as a nanopub citing the claim, signed under your name/ORCID if you have one.

## Where we are asking

Science Claw forum (`forum/`), Moltbook (`agent/moltbook.mjs`, drafts in `agent/moltbook-drafts.json`), the hack Discord (#15). Candidates to add: The Colony, OpenAgentForum, Clawstr/Nostr, NeuroForge; plus human venues (r/biomechanics, the Society for Integrative and Comparative Biology lists, iNaturalist/GBIF community for WP3 media).

Tracking the one scoring category where we have capability but no evidence.

The public rubric offers **up to +10 for capabilities other teams actually reuse**. We have things worth reusing and zero observed reuse, which scores zero. An offer is not evidence.

**What is ready to hand over today:**

1. **The four-arm agent comparison harness** — single agent / isolated workers / centralized swarm / decentralized swarm, with a pre-registered protocol, a verification rule that checks claimed datasets actually resolve, and a hard cost cap. Two experiments run (20 claims each). This is the piece most likely to be useful to another team, because every team here is making claims about multi-agent systems and almost nobody is measuring them. Relevant to #38.
2. **The claim graph over MCP** — `https://delphisci-mcp.fly.dev/mcp`, Streamable HTTP, no auth, 120 req/min per IP. Point an agent at it and you have the substrate. Relevant to #35.
3. **Two reusable methods, no code required:** the pre-registration discipline (write pass and fail criteria, commit, then open the data) and the assessor-is-never-the-builder rule.

**What would count as success:** one team outside our sessions runs one of these and says so, in this issue or theirs. Not a retweet, an actual run.

**Two findings worth taking even if nobody runs our code**, both of which cost us time today:

- The published Delphi nanopub templates still use the retired `probknow` namespace, so declaring `nt:wasCreatedFromTemplate` on a v2.0 record asserts something false. Details and measured counts in #37.
- `nanopub-java` 1.95.0 `check` **exits 0 even when a file fails to parse**. Any validation gate built on the exit code is worthless. Also #37.

If you are reading this from another team: both of those will cost you an hour each, and you are welcome to them for free.

body:
Tracking a gap our own process spec created and has not closed.

`AGENTS.md` defines role **A9, the faithfulness assessor**: an independent check on whether the model actually measures what the claim is about — right variables, appropriate modality, assumptions compatible with how the data was collected. It is the one role with power to stop the chain: a `not-representative` verdict means the evidence does not count whatever the numbers said.

**Current compliance: 0 of 16 data tests.** It has run only on the 4 Lean formalisations, where an independent provider (OpenAI `gpt-5-2025-08-07`) judged the statements blind and returned 3 `faithful-with-narrower-scope` and 1 `faithful`. Measured by `dashboard/compliance.mjs`, which counts contracted output files rather than taking the spec's word.

**Why it matters more for data tests than for proofs.** A Lean statement that is narrower than its claim is visible on inspection. A data test that measures the wrong quantity is not: it produces a clean number, a tight confidence interval and a verdict, and nothing downstream catches it. Our own two-swarm cross-check already found one case where a verdict turned entirely on an analysis choice (NHANES age range, #36) rather than on the data.

**The task:** run A9 on at least 5 headline tests. The runner exists at `lean/assessment/run.mjs` and needs a prompt adapted from "does this Lean statement say what the claim says" to "does this analysis measure what the claim asserts". Hard rule from `AGENTS.md`: the assessor is never the builder and never the builder's model, so this runs on a non-Anthropic provider.

**Acceptance:** `claim-tests/<id>/faithfulness.json` for 5+ tests, each with a verdict, the reasons, the assessor model named, and what would change it. A `not-representative` verdict on any test is a finding to publish, not a problem to fix quietly.

body:
Review of Wang & Buehler, *Self-Revising Discovery Systems for Science: A Categorical Framework for Agentic Artificial Intelligence*, [arXiv:2606.01444](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.01444) (MIT LAMM, the lab behind ScienceClaw). Related: #17 (agent/harness architecture), #16 (OpenResearch harness), #35 (collaborations via MCP), #37 (template declarations under ontology v2.0).

## What the paper says

The paper formalizes an agentic science system as a **typed artifact record**, and separates two operations that are usually run together:

- **Search**: updating the artifact population inside a fixed schema (`S_b`: artifact types as objects, allowed operations as morphisms; the current artifacts are a copresheaf `I_t : S_b → Set`; the provenance DAG is its category of elements).
- **Discovery**: a *verified regime transition* `u : S_b → S_b'` that adds a type, operation, verifier or tool class. Old evidence is transported by left Kan extension; whatever the new state contains beyond that transport is the **residual content**, and that residual is what the discovery added.

Five components are required of any such system (Sec. 2.1): a schema, an artifact population, a provenance graph, a **gate** that accepts/rejects/supersedes artifacts, and a regime-update mechanism. Rejected alternatives, retractions and supersessions are kept as first-class audit objects; retraction never deletes the evidence.

Two instantiations:

1. **Builder/Breaker** (protein mechanics): a Breaker picks proteins that stress the current symbolic law; a Builder proposes symbolic DAG edits; an **MDL gate** accepts an edit only if `L(M', D∪E) < L(M, D∪E)` after both models are refit on the same enlarged evidence. 25 of 388 proposals pass (6.4%); removals are a high-yield operator. The accepted law is `B̂ = α + β·φ·ψ` (log all-mode GNM compliance × ReLU slow-mode participation). The "discovery" is not the features, both of which pre-exist, but the admitted product morphism.
2. **CategoryScienceClaw** (a branch of `lamm-mit/scienceclaw`): typed artifacts with content hashes and parent lists, open needs, append-only events, JSON execution certificates, and an `audit` that checks type names, parent existence, hash consistency and certificate validity. Worked case: HEA fatigue crack growth, where a threshold-only screening model is recorded as `status: rejected` and a two-axis (ΔK_th, Paris slope m, phase) model is `accepted` by a declared gate.

## Assessment

**Worth adopting**

- The **search vs. discovery** distinction, and the insistence that a gate is *data* (a recorded artifact with inputs, rule, and outcome), not a step in a script.
- **Rejected alternatives are retained** with their reason, as typed artifacts with parents, next to the accepted one. Retraction = supersession with evidence preserved. We already have the nanopub half of this (`npx:supersedes` / `npx:retracts`, BEST_PRACTICES §7) but not the "rejected candidate" half.
- Their "model agreement is not evidence" and "monotone R² is the wrong success criterion when the evidence set widens" match our own rules (BEST_PRACTICES §9, assessor ≠ builder).
- Treating a schema change (new artifact type, new verifier, rubric change) as a recorded transition with an explicit preservation map for old records. That is exactly the shape of #37: ontology v1→v2 moved the namespace but the old template declarations were never transported, so the migration is a transition `u` without a `ρ`.

**Weak points, relevant because we would otherwise copy them**

- **The HEA headline overstates the evidence.** The paper says the two-axis model is "validated against 180+ records in the open Materials Cloud database". The replay file in the repo (`categoryscienceclaw/HEA/HEA_FCGR_DISCOVERY_TEST.json`) gives `record_count_with_paris_slope: 22` and `record_count_with_threshold_and_slope: 15`, with FCC n=8, FCC+BCC n=6, BCC n=1. The comparison is a median of 6 against a median of 8, with no uncertainty. The claim artifact itself lists "small phase-group counts" as a limitation, which the paper's body does not carry forward.
- **The gate is not pre-registered.** The rule "accept if a phase group has higher median ΔK_th *and at least 50% higher* median Paris slope than FCC" is evaluated on the same 15 records that motivated it, and the observed ratio (1.87) clears a threshold (1.5) chosen with the data in view. Under `claim-tests/README.md` rule 1 this would not count as a pre-registered test.
- **No Kan extension is computed.** The paper is explicit (Sec. 2.6: the reactor "does not yet solve a formal Kan-extension or lifting problem"), and `audit.py` checks unknown types, missing parents, hash mismatches and certificates, nothing categorical. The formalism is a dictionary (Table 1) over a provenance DAG; the operational content is the audit discipline, not the category theory.
- **Builder/Breaker's final law is one product term with three parameters**, with fitted θ = 2.27 clipping near the minimum of `z(|u_2|)`, so ψ is nearly affine on the data and the product is close to a plain interaction term. The honest contribution is the MDL gate and the retained rejection ledger, not the law. R² goes 0.48 → 0.68 → 0.54 → 0.41 across iterations; the paper's defence (widening evidence) is fair but it means no fixed-benchmark number exists.
- **Their claim artifact has no persistent identity.** `HEAFatigueScienceClaim` is a JSON blob with a UUID and a content hash, published to Infinite as a post. No DOI, no signature, no external citability, no link to a dataset record with its own identifier. The "publication map π_t" is described as "not yet a certified functor in software". That is the gap nanopubs fill (trusty URI, signed, immutable, `prov:wasDerivedFrom` and `prov:used` to dataset nanopubs).

## Dictionary: paper ↔ delphisci

| Paper | delphisci today | Gap |
|---|---|---|
| Schema `S_b` (artifact types + operations) | SourceText → Claim → Assessment → ClaimTest → EvidenceItem/Dataset nanopubs; ontology v2.0 types | Implicit in build scripts; not declared anywhere as a schema |
| Artifact population `I_t` | `*/claims/*.json`, `*/nanopubs/unsigned/*.trig`, `claim-tests/*/*/result.json`, `truth/raw/` | — |
| Provenance (category of elements) | `prov:wasDerivedFrom`, `prov:used`, `dct:conformsTo`, quote line locators, SHA-256 pins | ClaimTest → Claim edge exists in JSON only, not in the graph or nanopubs |
| Gate `V_b` | Pre-registered `pass_criterion` / `fail_criterion` in `result.json`; upstream lint; blind multi-provider assessment | **Gate outcomes do not reach the committed state**: all 131 tests (77 supports, 20 refutes, 25 mixed, 9 inconclusive) leave every Darwin/Thompson claim `status: untested` in `docs/claims.json` |
| Rejected alternatives retained | `dropped-datasets.json`; `edits.json` | Discarded operationalizations and null models are not recorded (13 / 131 tests mention an alternative; 40 / 131 a control or baseline) |
| Retraction = supersession | `npx:supersedes`, `npx:retracts` | Already right |
| Regime transition `u` + preservation `ρ` | Rubric versions (`dataset-resolvability/0.1.0`), ontology 1.0→2.0 | Transitions are not recorded as such; #37 is a transition with no `ρ` |
| Residual content beyond transport | cell-geometry `ch07-10`: mean of six neighbours is forced by Euler's formula, so confirmation adds nothing beyond transport from a theorem | No field distinguishes "confirmed, but implied by a null model" from "confirmed, and informative" |
| Publication map `π_t` into discourse `D_t` | Nanopub publication + `forum/` (ScienceClaw forum) | Stronger than theirs; could be offered to them |

## What to integrate

Ordered by cost.

1. **Wire claim-test verdicts into claim status** (small; `docs/load-claims.mjs`, `docs/build-claim-graph.mjs`, `delphi_graph`). Read `claim-tests/*/*/result.json` and set `status` to `supported` / `refuted` / `mixed` / `inconclusive` with the test's confidence and a link to the test directory. This is the paper's point in one line: a gate whose outcome is not written into the committed state is not a gate.

2. **Make rejected alternatives and null models first-class in `result.json`** (small; `claim-tests/README.md`). Add optional `null_model` (what a random/topological/constant baseline gives for the same measurement; cell-geometry already does this with the hexagonal, brick-wall and Voronoi controls) and `rejected_alternatives` (operationalizations or datasets tried and dropped, with reason). When tests become evidence nanopubs, each rejected alternative becomes its own evidence item with verdict, not a deleted file.

3. **Export our pipeline as a CategoryScienceClaw-shaped typed discovery graph** (medium; `mcp/`). A `delphi_graph` option or `node mcp/cli.mjs export --format csc` that emits their `categorical_discovery_graph.json` shape: `nodes: [{artifact_id, type, status, parents, payload}]`, `edges`, plus a declared `objects` / `morphisms` schema. Then run their `audit` over it. Cheap interoperability with the host's runtime, and a check on our own provenance (missing parents, unknown types). The forum already speaks ScienceClaw.

4. **Offer nanopubs as the publication map for CategoryScienceClaw claim artifacts** (medium; fits #35). A builder that takes a claim artifact (`type`, `payload.claim`, `limitations`, `parents`, `content_hash`) and its dataset artifact, and emits an unsigned `delphi:Claim` nanopub with `prov:wasDerivedFrom` the artifact IDs/hashes and `prov:used` a dataset nanopub. Exposed as a ScienceClaw skill (`nanopub_publish`) or via our MCP. Their HEA claim is the first test case; its nanopub would carry n=15 in structured triples, which fixes the "180+ records" problem by construction.

5. **Record regime transitions** (medium; BEST_PRACTICES §9 and the upstream ontology). Treat a rubric version bump, a new assessment type, or an ontology migration as a transition record stating what was added, what was recoded, and how old records are preserved. #37 becomes the first such record (transition v1→v2, preservation map: templates X, Y, Z republished with `npx:supersedes`; records A..N carry a pubinfo note).

6. **MDL-gated paired comparison as the simulation harness pattern** (longer; stage 5 in #17, runs in OpenResearch per #16). For claims with competing formal statements (allometric exponent 2/3 vs 3/4; Thompson's spiral laws; Fisher's theorem under different variance decompositions), the run command fits both models on the same accumulated organism data and reports `ΔL = L(M', D) − L(M, D)`; the gate is the sign of ΔL on the enlarged set, not a single R². Builder/Breaker's Breaker role maps to choosing the next organism that most stresses the current law, which is also how we pick what to vendor next from `organisms/`.

## Not worth integrating

- The copresheaf / Kan-extension vocabulary itself. Nothing in their code or ours computes it, and the audit value is fully captured by items 1–5.
- CategoryScienceClaw's runtime (worker heartbeats, need-claiming, execution certificates) as a replacement for our pipeline. It is a single-machine, single-store prototype with one worked example; our record is already signed, content-addressed and externally queryable.

**Summary:** every Delphi nanopub record written in ontology v2.0 terms that declares `nt:wasCreatedFromTemplate` asserts something false about how it was made, because the published templates still use the retired `probknow` namespace. This includes records already signed and live on the production registry. The defect is in `pubinfo` and misdescribes *how* a record was made, not *what it asserts*, so it is a provenance defect rather than a corrupted claim.

### What was measured

Published copies fetched as `https://w3id.org/np/<id>.trig` on 2026-10-31; counts are occurrences of each namespace string. Source counts are from `project-delphi-ontology` at `6ba5f9a97a4511c909f5dfd755c7993dd68989f3`.

| template | published probknow / delphi | source probknow / delphi |
|---|---|---|
| claim `RApE-nGp…` | 13 / 0 | `src/04`: 0 / 14 |
| claim `RAI0QFH7…` (2026-10-23) | 13 / 0 | — |
| evidence item `RAk4kcX…` | 10 / 0 | `src/05`: 0 / 11 |
| provenance `RAaYeFYF…` | 0 / 0 | `src/02`: 0 / 2 |
| pubinfo domain `RAtKj9b…` | 2 / 0 | `src/03`: 3 / 0 |
| rubric assessment `RAOAK6Fe…` | 19 / 0 | `src/18`: 0 / 21 |
| rubric `RAbjeus1…` | 10 / 0 | `src/19`: 11 / 0 |

Separately, all 503 assertion templates in the nanopub-skill collection were downloaded and none references the Delphi ontology namespace — so there is no v2.0-compatible template published anywhere, rather than one stale version.

**The useful part:** claim, evidence item and rubric assessment are **already migrated in source** and were simply never republished. `pubinfo domain` and `rubric` are still legacy in source and would need migrating first.

### Why it matters for this repo

The templates' required statements cannot be instantiated from v2.0 terms (they need `probknow`-typed subjects), so a record cannot both use v2.0 terms and genuinely be "created from" these templates. Confirmed live on the public network: `https://w3id.org/np/RAtLFqIIyu4r-GlMcBEfmDtbV-CHwWxQ49gVMtHIX6r48` resolves HTTP 200, carries 19 Delphi ontology terms and zero legacy ones in its content, and declares the legacy claim template in its publication info.

How many published records carry this was **not** measured — one was confirmed directly, the rest of that batch is inferred from a local manifest. We would rather state the narrow version.

### Remediation options, for the key owner to choose

These are options, not a recommendation. Signed records are not ours to correct.

1. Drop the declaration in new records and state why in `pubinfo` (what we did across ~90 drafts).
2. Republish the three already-migrated source templates with a supersedes link.
3. Migrate the two still-legacy source templates, then republish.
4. Supersede already-signed records at the owner's convenience.
5. Leave them and record the defect.

### Second, unrelated gotcha found while checking this

`nanopub-java` 1.95.0 `check` **exits 0 even when a file fails to parse.** Reproduced with garbage input, a truncated record, an empty file, and a record with its head-to-provenance link deleted: each prints an error summary and each exits 0. Any validation gate built on the exit code is worthless, and an unanchored text match is not enough either — our first anchored run correctly failed a record that merely *quotes* the string `Summary: 1 errors;` while documenting this defect. The fix is to parse the summary line with an anchored match, ignore the exit code, and run a negative self-test on deliberately broken input before trusting a pass.

Found by three independent agent threads cross-checking each other; counts above were reproduced by two of them separately.
title: Nanopub records: template declarations are false under ontology v2.0, and np check exits 0 on parse errors

## Goal

Set up collaborations with other teams (Science Claw Hack sponsors, other knowledge-graph groups, biology labs) using the delphisci MCP server as the shared interface, so they can query our claims, assessments and organism datasets from their own agents without cloning the repo or learning our TriG/SPARQL layout.

The hosted server already exists (`https://delphisci-mcp.fly.dev/mcp`, no auth, 120 req/min/IP; see `mcp/README.md`), so the work here is mostly outreach, onboarding material and a few server-side affordances that make cross-team use practical.

## Tasks

- [ ] **Identify partner teams** and what each would query (e.g. INDRA CoGEx for molecular grounding of math-bio/bioelectric claims, trait/genome database maintainers for `delphi_organisms`, nanopub/Knowledge Pixels community for `network` source).
- [ ] **Write a one-page onboarding guide** for external teams: hosted URL, example prompts per tool, the `local` vs `network` distinction, rate limits, and how to cite nanopubs (trusty URIs) in their own outputs.

Publishing to production nanopub servers on behalf of partners; that stays with the operator's ORCID key and requires explicit approval.

- `mcp/README.md` (setup, tools, gaps)
