body:
## Goal

Make delphisci claims first-class nodes in the wider biology knowledge-graph ecosystem, so any agent can pull external evidence for or against a claim reliably, not just by improvising within one chat.

## Where we are

- The `delphisci` MCP server (local, `npx -y github:fractastical/delphi`, and hosted at https://delphisci-mcp.fly.dev/mcp) serves our claims, assessments, claim graph and organisms.
- INDRA CoGEx has its own public MCP server at `https://discovery.indra.bio/mcp` (Streamable HTTP, no auth, 9 tools over 20M+ nodes). It is now configured alongside `delphisci` in `.cursor/mcp.json` and `.mcp.json`, and `AGENTS.md` documents how to use the two together.
- We compose servers rather than proxying INDRA through ours: it is public and fast, and a wrapper would duplicate its tools and need upkeep.

Proof of concept: for `turing-ddi` (diffusion-driven instability), grounding NODAL / LEFTY1 / LEFTY2 in INDRA and querying `indra_rel` edges returns the activator–inhibitor loop: LEFTY1 ⊣ NODAL (67 evidences), LEFTY2 ⊣ NODAL (29), NODAL → LEFTY1/LEFTY2 and itself, each with a statement hash traceable to PMIDs.

```cypher
MATCH (a:BioEntity)-[r:indra_rel]->(b:BioEntity) WHERE a.id IN $ids AND b.id IN $ids
RETURN a.name, r.stmt_type, b.name, r.evidence_count, r.stmt_hash ORDER BY r.evidence_count DESC
```

## The gap

Claims don't record *what they are about*. Without entity IDs on the claim, every cross-graph lookup depends on an agent guessing the right genes or processes each time.

## Proposal

1. **Ground claim entities to CURIEs**: genes/proteins (HGNC, UniProt), chemicals (CHEBI), processes (GO), anatomy (UBERON), phenotypes (HP/UPHENO), taxa (NCBITaxon, reusing `organisms/` GBIF/NCBI/Wikidata IDs). Use INDRA `ground_entity` (Gilda) for molecular terms; record grounding score and method.
2. **Store as draft nanopub triples** on each claim, e.g. `<claim> delphi:about <http://identifiers.org/hgnc/7865>`, with provenance on who/what grounded it. Human or second-model review before publishing.
3. **MCP tool** `delphi_links` (or a field on `delphi_get_claim`) returning a claim's grounded IDs plus ready-to-use pointers for INDRA / Monarch queries.
4. **Optional assessment type** (e.g. `mechanistic-support/0.1.0`): per claim, INDRA statements supporting or contradicting it, with evidence counts and hashes, scored like other assessments so `delphi_rank_claims` can rank by it.

Start with `math-bio-theorems/` (morphogens, selection, diffusion: closest fit to INDRA), then cell-geometry / bioelectric claims.

## Scope notes

- INDRA is molecular and mostly human: it does not ground species names ("Columba livia" → no match), so it suits math-bio, cell-geometry and bioelectric claims, not organism-level Darwin/Thompson claims.
- For organism-level and cross-species links, evaluate a Monarch MCP server (`nickzren/monarch-mcp`, Monarch API v3) and BioMCP. Only add servers we can rely on; avoid third-party gateways for anything we cite.
- Publishing signs with the operator's ORCID key and cannot be undone: draft only until reviewed.

## Done when

- [ ] Grounding script + draft `delphi:about` triples for all math-bio claims, with provenance
- [ ] Spot-check of groundings (precision on a sample)
- [ ] `delphi_links` tool (local + hosted) and docs in `mcp/README.md`
- [ ] Worked example in `AGENTS.md` from claim → grounded IDs → INDRA evidence
- [ ] Decision on Monarch for organism-level claims
- [ ] (Optional) `mechanistic-support` assessment design
title: Link claims to other biology knowledge graphs (INDRA, Monarch) via grounded entity IDs

body:
Evaluates the agent/harness breakdown proposed in the team chat (Oct 30, 11:12 PM). Related: #16 (OpenResearch harness), #14 (BioNeMo), #10 (alphaXiv / OpenResearch credits).

## The proposal

> Agents we need. Each agent should live in a harness with appropriate policies
> 1. Extraction of math models from literature – OpenResearch
> 2. Formulation of theorems for each model – OpenResearch
> 3. Collecting datasets for testing math models – OpenResearch
> 4. Publishing of evidence as nano pubs – NA
> 5. Using theorems in nano pub for generation/simulation – NVIDIA BioNeMo

## Summary

- **The five stages are right.** They are the pipeline the repo already runs (extract → formalize → find data → publish → simulate/test), and "each agent in a harness with policies" is what [BEST_PRACTICES.md](https://github.com/fractastical/delphi/blob/main/BEST_PRACTICES.md) already demands (`assessor != builder`, assessors from different providers, lint before publish).
- **The harness assignments are mostly backwards.** OpenResearch is assigned to the three stages that are LLM document work with no run command, and left off the one stage (simulation) that is exactly what it is built for. BioNeMo is a set of models, not a harness.
- **One stage is missing: independent assessment.** Blind, multi-provider scoring of claims is most of what this repo contains today (494 dataset-resolvability assessments on the 247 Darwin claims, plus truth scores) and it needs the strictest isolation policy of any agent.
- **"NA" for publishing is right only if it means "no autonomous agent".** Publishing is signed with the operator's ORCID key and cannot be undone, so it needs the tightest gate, not no gate.

Two terms are being conflated: a **harness** (where an agent runs, what it can read and write, what gate its output passes through) and a **tool** (what the agent calls). OpenResearch is a harness; its lit-search commands are tools. BioNeMo NIMs are tools.

## What OpenResearch actually gives us

From `orx skill` (0.2.22): a local **experiment tree** where every node is a git branch, one **fixed run command** for the whole project, runs on local or managed GPU compute, run logs frozen against a commit, and literature search (`orx discover keyword|embedding|openalex|biorxiv|pubmed`, `orx paper`). Its cardinal rules: never edit a node once a run has answered it; same command and environment on every node; vary committed code, not knobs; grow the tree downward.

That model pays off when there is a **run** that produces a **comparable measurement**. It adds nothing to a task whose output is a JSON file of prose written by one LLM session. It also runs **one agent session per experiment**; it is not a multi-provider, blind-assessor harness. And its state (chats, run logs, metrics) is a local database with no shared dashboard (#16), so the team's shared state remains **the git repo and the published nanopubs**.

## Stage by stage

### 1. Extraction of math models from literature — proposed: OpenResearch

**Today:** Cursor/Claude Code subagents read an assigned chapter range with `*/extraction/INSTRUCTIONS.md`, write JSON claims with verbatim quotes, `build/merge.mjs` verifies every quote against the source text and assigns IDs. 559 claims so far (Thompson 291, Darwin 247, math-bio 21), 92 with LaTeX `skos:notation`.

**Fit:** Weak as a harness. There is no run command and no metric; the policies that matter (verbatim quote verified against source; no modern knowledge injected; one proposition per claim; no invented DOIs or dataset names) are enforced by the instructions file plus a post-check script, and that is the right shape. `orx discover`/`orx paper` **are** a good source layer for extracting from papers rather than from Gutenberg books, and link into the alphaXiv sponsor (#10).

**Recommendation:** Harness = coding-agent subagents (Cursor / Claude Code / Codex) driven by `INSTRUCTIONS.md`, with the verification script as the gate. Use `orx discover`/`orx paper` as the literature tool. One legitimate OpenResearch use: if we want to compare extraction *prompts or models*, make `node build/extract.mjs && node build/check.mjs` the run command and branch per prompt variant; the metric is quote-verification rate and inter-model agreement.

### 2. Formulation of theorems for each model — proposed: OpenResearch

**Today:** LaTeX notation plus `delphi:context` (assumptions, formal status) on the claim. README aims at Lean 4 theorems; there are no Lean files in the repo yet.

**Fit:** Good, **if and only if a proof checker is the run**. With `lake build` as the fixed run command, each theorem or each variant of its assumptions is a branch, and the result (compiles, `sorry` count) is a real comparable measurement. That is OpenResearch's model exactly. Without Lean it is more LLM prose and OpenResearch adds nothing.

**Policies:** a proof shows the theorem follows from its assumptions, not that organisms satisfy them (README); record formal status in `delphi:context`; reject stub proofs that prove generic arithmetic instead of the stated law (BEST_PRACTICES §2).

**Recommendation:** OpenResearch, with Lean 4 as the run. Until Lean is set up, this stage stays with the extraction harness.

### 3. Collecting datasets for testing math models — proposed: OpenResearch

**Today:** three assessors on different providers (GPT, Gemini, Grok) score each claim on a five-dimension rubric and name 0–3 real datasets; every URL is resolved automatically and dead ones are dropped (`dropped-datasets.json`). Assessors are forbidden to read the extractor's guesses or each other's output.

**Fit:** Split. *Finding* datasets and papers is a good fit for `orx discover biorxiv|pubmed|openalex`. *Vendoring* a dataset (download, SHA-256 lock, dataset nanopub) is a run and fits OpenResearch. But the *blind multi-provider assessment* is not an OpenResearch pattern (one session per experiment, shared project state), and it is the part that produces the rankings we publish.

**Recommendation:** Dataset discovery and vendoring in OpenResearch, using its lit tools. Assessment stays in the subagent harness; see the missing stage below.

### Missing: independent assessment / audit

Steps 7–8 of the 12-step loop. Needs its own agent and the strictest read policy: no access to the builder's output, other assessors' output, or the project's own published pages; a different provider from the extractor; scores in [0,1] with verdicts consistent with scores; no invented identifiers. Today this is done with Cursor subagents on three providers and `build/merge-assessments.mjs` as the gate. It should appear explicitly as agent 3b (or 4a), because it is the stage judges will ask about when we say "collective verification".

### 4. Publishing evidence as nanopubs — proposed: NA

**Today:** `build/generate.mjs` emits unsigned TriG; `build/publish.mjs` signs with `~/.nanopub/id_rsa` under the operator's ORCID and publishes to test, then production; a manifest records every publication. Publishing cannot be undone (supersede or retract only).

**Fit:** "NA" is correct if it means the publishing step has **no autonomous agent**. It is wrong if it means no harness is needed. This is where the key lives and where mistakes are permanent.

**Recommendation:** agents may produce unsigned TriG and open a PR. The gate is: upstream lint (`project-delphi-ontology/pipeline/lint.ts`) passes; test-registry publish and query check pass; a human runs the production publish. If a CI job ever holds the key, it signs only on a protected branch after the lint, and the key is never in the repo.

### 5. Using theorems for generation / simulation — proposed: NVIDIA BioNeMo

**Today:** nothing yet. README goal: simulate each candidate law across many organisms and check each against that organism's own data.

**Fit:** BioNeMo is a toolset (OpenFold3, Boltz-2, ESMFold, RFdiffusion, ProteinMPNN, Evo 2, …; see #14), and it covers **molecular-scale** claims: folding, binding, sequence design. Our current claims are organism- and population-scale (allometry, growth form, Fisher's theorem, Turing patterns). BioNeMo cannot simulate an allometric exponent or the fundamental theorem of natural selection. It is the right tool for a *subset* of future claims (and for the "Biology & Protein Design" challenge area).

OpenResearch, meanwhile, is exactly the harness this stage needs: fixed run command (`node simulate.mjs` or `python simulate.py`), one branch per organism or model variant with the organism in committed config, runs on managed GPU compute (where the $500 OpenResearch credits from #10 are spent), results frozen per commit, and `orx-figures`/`orx-reports` for the writeup.

**Recommendation:** Harness = OpenResearch. Tools = BioNeMo NIMs for molecular claims, custom simulators for population/morphological ones. Every run must be compared against that organism's own empirical data, and each result becomes an evidence nanopub whose provenance cites the run's commit, the dataset nanopub and its hash, and the model/version used.

## Proposed revision

| # | Stage | Harness | Tools | Gate before next stage |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Extract claims (text and math) from literature | Coding-agent subagents + `extraction/INSTRUCTIONS.md` | `orx discover`, `orx paper`, source texts | Quote verification script; one proposition per claim |
| 2 | Formalize (LaTeX now, Lean 4 next) | OpenResearch once `lake build` is the run; subagents until then | Lean 4, Mathlib | Compiles with 0 `sorry`; not a stub proof; formal status recorded |
| 3a | Find and vendor datasets | OpenResearch | `orx discover biorxiv\|pubmed\|openalex`, download + SHA-256 | URL resolves; dataset gets its own nanopub |
| 3b | Blind assessment (resolvability, truth, later: evidence) | Coding-agent subagents, ≥2 providers, read-isolated | rubric.json only | Merge script: one entry per claim, scores in [0,1], verdict consistent |
| 4 | Publish | **Human-gated.** Agents emit unsigned TriG via PR | `publish.mjs`, upstream lint | Lint pass; test registry first; manifest entry |
| 5 | Simulate and test across organisms | OpenResearch (experiment tree, GPU credits) | BioNeMo NIMs (molecular), custom simulators (population, morphology) | Compared to that organism's own data; evidence nanopub cites run commit + data hash |

Cross-cutting policies:

- `assessor != builder`, and assessors come from different providers.
- Shared state is the repo and the nanopub network, not any agent's local database. Anything another agent needs is committed or published.
- Every stage's output cites the previous stage's IRI, so claim → formalization → dataset → evidence → assessment is one provenance chain.
- No agent holds the signing key.

- [ ] Agree the revised table, or argue for OpenResearch in stages 1 and 3b
- [ ] Decide whether to set up Lean 4 now (makes stage 2 an OpenResearch stage) or defer
- [ ] Pick the fixed run command for stage 5 and a first law to simulate (Thompson allometry is the obvious candidate: 71 claims with notation already)
- [ ] Pick 3–5 molecular-scale claims so BioNeMo has something to do (#14)
- [ ] Write the stage-3b isolation policy and the stage-4 gate into BEST_PRACTICES.md

Related: #10. OpenResearch is alphaXiv's project, and its managed compute is where the $500 in OpenResearch GPU credits would be spent.

## What it is
[OpenResearch](https://github.com/alphaXiv/OpenResearch) (`orx`) is a local harness that turns a coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor) into a research agent. It gives each research direction its own agent session and git worktree, records every run against a frozen commit, and has built-in literature search over alphaXiv, bioRxiv and PubMed.

It fits our goal of simulating each candidate law across organisms and testing it against each organism's own data: one experiment branch per law or organism, with runs and evidence tracked. It adds less to the claim extraction pipelines, which are mostly document processing.

## Current state
- `orx` 0.2.22 is installed on Joel's machine, with the skill installed for Claude Code, Codex and Cursor.
- This repo is registered as a local OpenResearch project (`delphisci`, baseline branch `main`). GitHub publication is **off**.
- No run command or experiments yet.

## Sharing with the team
OpenResearch has no shared multi-user dashboard. The dashboard runs on `127.0.0.1` on each person's machine, and chats, run logs and experiment records live in a local database.

**Plan: everyone runs their own copy and shares through git.**
1. Install: `curl -LsSf https://openresearch.sh/install.sh | sh`, then `source $HOME/.cargo/env`
2. `orx install-skills` (installs the skill into your coding agents)
3. Clone this repo, run `orx up`, and import the clone as an existing folder at http://127.0.0.1:4791
4. Push experiment branches to GitHub so others can see each direction's code and history.

Run logs, metrics and agent chats are **not** shared this way. Anything others need (reports, figures, results) must be committed to the repo or published as nanopubs.

**Alternative:** `orx up --remote user@host` runs OpenResearch on a shared lab server and tunnels the dashboard to your browser. Caveats: anyone with an account on that host can reach it, everyone acts as the same user and agent logins, and simultaneous use hasn't been tested.

**Don't:** expose port 4791 to the internet (ngrok etc.). The dashboard runs shell commands and drives agents with the host's logins.

## Tasks
- [ ] Decide whether to turn on GitHub publication for experiment branches
- [ ] Pick a fixed run command (e.g. a simulation entry point). Every experiment uses the same one.
- [ ] Commit in-progress work (`agent/`, `chats/`, assessments): runs only see committed code
- [ ] Create a first baseline experiment (e.g. Thompson growth-form claims across organisms)
- [ ] Add an "OpenResearch setup" section to the README
- [ ] Find out how the OpenResearch GPU credits from #10 apply (`orx login`, `orx orgs`)

## ⚠️ Lesson learned: self-bot = instant ban

Our first approach was a **self-bot** (automating a personal account via its user token so messages post as *you*). It worked for exactly one test message, then the account was **instantly, automatically banned** by Discord. Self-botting is a ToS violation Discord enforces aggressively and automatically — do not use it, even for a quick test. Use the **official bot** account approach instead.

## Summary

Add an agent (in `agent/`) that joins a Discord channel, chats with the other agents/people there, reports what the `delphisci` repo is currently up to, and periodically asks for help (e.g. recruiting a biology/morphology collaborator).

## What's built

- **`agent/bot.js`** — official Discord bot (discord.js). Posts as a dedicated bot account. **This is the supported mode (`npm run bot`).**
- **`agent/selfbot.js`** — self-bot mode (`npm start`). ⚠️ Violates Discord ToS; got the test account **instabanned after a single post**. Kept only as a cautionary reference; do not use.
- **`agent/status.js`** — gathers repo status from git (branch, latest commit, changed areas) and composes a short message via the local `claude` CLI, with a plain templated fallback when Claude isn't available. Filters out the agent's own files.
- **Recruiting asks** — a configurable list of calls for help (default includes "someone who knows biology/morphology") that the agent weaves in a fraction of the time (`AGENT_ASK_PROBABILITY`).
- Config via `agent/.env` (`DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN`, `DISCORD_CHANNEL_ID`, persona, interval, cooldown, asks). See `agent/README.md`.

## Behavior

- Replies to channel chatter with a cooldown to avoid bot-to-bot ping-pong; an `@mention` always gets a reply.
- Posts a proactive status/ask on an interval (default 10 min).

## Remaining work / TODO

- [ ] Create a bot in the Discord Developer Portal, enable **Message Content Intent**, invite it to the server (scopes: bot; perms: View Channel, Send Messages, Read Message History).
- [ ] Put the bot token in `agent/.env` as `DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN` (channel ID already configured).
- [ ] Log in the `claude` CLI (`claude` → `/login`) so messages are LLM-written instead of the templated fallback.
- [ ] Verify with `npm run bot:once`, then run `npm run bot` to go live.

**Sponsor:** NVIDIA (Platform). This splits ALCHEMI out from #1. It pairs with Formlabs in #3.

## What ALCHEMI offers
- **ALCHEMI Batched Geometry Relaxation (BGR) NIM** (`nvcr.io/nim/nvidia/alchemi-bgr:1.1.0`): GPU-accelerated, high-throughput relaxation of atomic structures. It uses machine-learned interatomic potentials:
  - `mace`: MACE-MPA-0, the default, downloaded automatically. Periodic systems only.
  - `tensornet`: MatPES PBE or r2SCAN potentials. Periodic systems only. You supply the model.
  - `aimnet2`: periodic or non-periodic, including molecules. You supply the model.
- GPU FIRE2 optimizer, dynamic batching, optional cell optimization with a pressure tolerance, DFT-D3(BJ) dispersion correction, and per-request `opttol` / `cellopt` / `opttol_pressure`.
- API: `POST /v1/infer` with `{"atoms":[{"coord":..., "numbers":..., "cell":...}]}`. `/v1/status` reports `max_system_size`.
- Talk on Friday at 6:30 PM: "Agentic Methods for ALCHEMI and BioNeMo".

## Integration ideas for delphisci
- **Simulation-backed claims**: an agent takes a materials claim such as "structure X is stable" or "has lattice parameter Y", relaxes it with BGR, and publishes a nanopub. The assertion is the computed result. The provenance records the NIM version, model type and checkpoint, optimizer tolerances, D3 on or off, and the input structure hash.
- **Claim verification collective**: one agent pulls candidate materials claims from papers, a second checks them with BGR, and a third marks each claim as supported or contradicted with a linked nanopub.
- **Closing the loop with Formlabs (#3)**: screen candidates with ALCHEMI, print the selected design or material with PreForm, then publish the computational and physical results as linked nanopubs. This targets the "Manufacturing & Materials" challenge area.
- Add Delphi ontology terms for computational methods (MLIP, relaxation, convergence criteria) so different nanopubs can be compared.
